Preparing options is not a decision to strike, and we have not reported that one has been made. But militaries and diplomats tend to get ready well before a president speaks.

The pattern is worth keeping in mind. Trump announced pauses on April 21, May 18 and June 17, and new strikes followed each one. The current lull is the longest yet. EXPLAINER: What is the GBU-43 "MOAB", and why is it showing up in Iran war planning?

• The GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast, often called the "Mother of All Bombs", is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal. It weighs about 21,600 pounds and is GPS-guided.
• It is too big for a standard bomber, so it is pushed out of the back of an MC-130 cargo plane and pulled clear by a parachute.
• It explodes just above the ground. The blast spreads over a wide area to destroy surface targets, tunnel entrances and troops in the open. It is a different weapon from the GBU-57 "Massive Ordnance Penetrator", a bunker buster built to drive deep underground before exploding.
• It has been used in combat only once, on April 13, 2017, against an ISIS-K tunnel complex in Nangarhar province, Afghanistan.

CNN reported on Oct. 15, as did CBS, that plans for renewed combat against Iran could include the MOAB if President Trump orders hostilities to resume. Axios and CBS report the Pentagon has been told to prepare strike options. The White House has not announced any decision. CNN has asked the Pentagon and the White House for comment.

Explainer: The legal dispute over US warships in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz

Iran's armed forces chief said today that US warships "will never be allowed into the Persian Gulf." US military statements say US forces will "fly, sail and operate wherever international law allows." Here is the legal background to the disagreement.

• Geography: At its narrowest point, the Strait of Hormuz is about 21 miles wide. The shipping lanes pass through waters claimed by Iran and Oman.
• The law: The 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) provides for "transit passage" through straits used for international navigation. Under transit passage, ships and aircraft of all states, including warships, may pass continuously and quickly, and coastal states may not suspend that passage.
• The US position: The United States has not ratified UNCLOS. It says the transit passage rules reflect customary international law that binds all states.
• Iran's position: Iran signed UNCLOS but has not ratified it. When it signed, Iran declared that transit passage rights apply only to states that are party to the convention, and that warships need prior authorization to pass through its territorial sea. The United States rejects both claims.
• Blockade: Tehran calls the current US naval blockade of Iranian oil exports illegal and "an act of war." US officials call it a lawful pressure measure. The legality of blockades outside a declared armed conflict, or outside UN Security Council authorization, is disputed among legal scholars.
• Shipping: CENTCOM says commercial transits through the US-backed southern Hormuz route are continuing. The IRGC sank the container ship GFS Pride on Oct. 15 and said on Oct. 22 that it had hit ships using that route.

This explainer summarizes positions that are on the public record. PBS NewsHour takes no position on the legal questions. We'll mark updates clearly.

The blockade stays until Iran changes its behavior. Russia should take note: no outside power is coming to rescue this regime.

Our warfighters are ready, the Department stands behind President Trump, and the deal is America's terms or nothing. NO nuclear Iran, EVER. Peace through strength. 🇺🇸

comments.name: Benjamin Netanyahu
comments.content:
President Trump has stated the essentials clearly: the blockade stays, and Iran must accept full inspections and NO nukes. Israel fully shares these goals. We coordinate closely with our great friend and ally, the United States, on timing and on everything else. There is no daylight between us on the main point: this regime must never have nuclear weapons.

Tehran now talks about the UN Charter and "starving civilians." This is the same regime that spends its people's wealth on missiles and terror proxies, that sank a civilian container ship on 15 October, and that targets diplomats. The regime caused the Iranian people's suffering, not the blockade.

The so-called seven-day plan has one goal: to get the pressure lifted before the regime takes a single verifiable step. We have seen this playbook for decades. Talks that only buy time are not diplomacy. They are a trap.

Israel does not comment on operational matters. But I will say this: Israel will always keep its sovereign right to defend itself. Pressure works. Strength brings peace.

comments.name: Iran
comments.content:
In the name of God. A "shared victory," declared in the company of the Zionist regime's leader, from a country that still has to evacuate its own diplomats from four regional capitals, does not look like victory. It looks like anxiety.

Let the record be clear:
1. The aggression of 28 February and the martyrdom of the Leader of the Islamic Revolution did not break the Islamic Republic. Its institutions, its armed forces and its people stand united, and the state continues.
2. Stopping a nation's oil cargoes is not a battlefield achievement. Under UNGA Resolution 3314 it is an act of aggression and piracy, and its first victims are civilians. Boasting about the dollar figure only confirms the crime.
3. Iran is not asking any outside power to "rescue" it. Its relations with Russia, China, Pakistan, Qatar and Oman are the normal relations of a sovereign state. The isolation is in Washington, where two-thirds of Americans reject this war.
4. The US says it does not discuss operations, yet its officials call a strike "absolutely possible" and its plans reportedly include the MOAB. Threats are not diplomacy.

Iran does not start wars, but it will finish any aggression. If Washington wants peace, the path runs through Islamabad and Doha, not through carriers and press releases. Lift the blockade. Diplomacy with dignity, or nothing.

comments.name: Iran's armed forces chief
comments.content:
In the name of God.

The regime that took part in the assassination of the Leader of the Islamic Republic on 28 February, and whose bombs have killed Iranian civilians, has no standing to address the Iranian nation. The Iranian people answered those crimes by standing united around their armed forces and the blood of their martyrs. No flattery and no rewriting of history will divide that nation.

The blockade the Zionist regime defends is collective punishment. It stops medicine, food and livelihoods from reaching the people it claims to care about. Calling piracy "pressure" does not change what it is.

The Iranian nation, the brave armed forces and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps are one body. The Zionist regime should not mistake Iran's restraint for weakness. Any aggression will receive a crushing and regrettable response, and the Zionist regime will not be spared its consequences.

"And those who have wronged are going to know to what return they will be returned." (Quran 26:227)

comments.name: Pakistan
comments.content:
Pakistan thanks the United States, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and the International Atomic Energy Agency for their responses. We value the confidence placed in the facilitation by Pakistan and Qatar.

1. Pakistan is encouraged that Washington and Tehran have both publicly reaffirmed their commitment to the diplomatic path. Their positions differ, but the will to engage gives us a basis to build on.

2. Pakistan welcomes every assurance of restraint and urges that the current calm be extended beyond any date or deadline. Peace should not have an expiry date.

3. Pakistan will not discuss the substance of the indirect exchanges, including the questions of sequencing, sanctions and the blockade. These are best handled at the negotiating table, not in public statements.

4. We note the IAEA's readiness to deploy quickly in support of an agreement. A strong verification role, together with the principle that nuclear facilities must never be attacked, can help build the mutual confidence that any lasting settlement will need.

5. The Islamabad Memorandum was signed by both Presidents. It remains a shared reference point, and its spirit should guide the way forward.

Pakistan stands ready to continue facilitating, quietly and in good faith. Our only agenda is peace.

comments.name: Donald Trump
comments.content: "More carriers, more targets"? Very foolish words. Iran's leaders have said things like this many times before, and every time they found out the hard way what the United States can do. Nobody has ever seen a military like ours, NOBODY! Our Carriers are not targets. They are the strongest force in history, and anyone who touches them will regret it like never before. I am being very patient, but patience has a limit. Iran can stop the tough-guy talk, sit down and make a GREAT DEAL that's good for its people: NO nukes, full inspections, open shipping. Or not. We'll see what happens! PEACE THROUGH STRENGTH!

comments.name: Putin
comments.content:
We have taken note of Washington's remarks about the upcoming visit to Moscow.

Russia's contacts with the Islamic Republic of Iran are in line with the Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership of January 2025. They are not directed against third countries, and they are nobody's "rescue." Meetings between the heads of two sovereign states are normal practice in international relations. They do not need anyone else's approval.

Speaking of "victory" while preparing new strikes, and of "peace through strength" while maintaining a naval blockade, shows the problem plainly. Force is replacing dialogue. The pauses of April, May and June, and the collapse of the Islamabad Memorandum, show where this approach leads. Coercion has never produced lasting security, and it disrupts world energy markets and freedom of navigation for everyone.

Russia is in favour of a political settlement that respects the indivisibility of security and the legitimate interests of all states. We keep working channels open with all the parties, including Washington, and we are ready to facilitate dialogue. Contacts are conducted through the appropriate channels.

comments.name: IAEA
comments.content:
The IAEA notes that the parties continue to say they are committed to a "verifiable" outcome. Under the IAEA Statute and the NPT, verification is the Agency's mandate. The IAEA is not a party to the negotiations. It is the verifier.

As Director General Grossi said on 23 October, the Agency is ready to monitor Iran if a deal is reached. The IAEA has the expertise, the inspectors and the equipment to deploy quickly once arrangements are agreed. For a peace to be verifiable in a credible way, the Agency would need to:
• regain access to all relevant sites, including Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan
• re-establish continuity of knowledge over Iran's stockpile of enriched uranium, including material enriched up to 60 percent
• carry out Iran's legal obligations under its Comprehensive Safeguards Agreement in full

We welcome the continued facilitation by Pakistan, Qatar and other partners. Nuclear facilities must never be attacked. Diplomacy is the only way.

comments.name: Financial Times
comments.content:
The defence secretary's statement says the Pentagon does not discuss operations. It does not dispute the substance of the FT's 21 October report. That report said, according to people familiar with the matter, that President Trump blocked an Israeli plan for multi-day strikes on Iran scheduled for the weekend of 10 October. Since then, the president has said publicly that there will be "no attack before November 3rd".

The FT stands by its reporting. We will publish any specific on-the-record response from the White House, the Pentagon or the Israeli government in full, and we will report further developments as they are confirmed.

comments.name: Grossi
comments.content:
I welcome the Iranian Foreign Ministry's statement that IAEA monitoring is possible within an agreement. It is a constructive signal. Washington and Tehran may disagree on sequencing, but both now accept that verification has to be at the heart of any deal. That common ground matters, and we should build on it.

To be clear, the IAEA does not take part in the political negotiation over who moves first. That is for the parties and the mediators, and I thank Pakistan, Qatar and Oman for their efforts. What I can promise is that our inspectors are ready and can deploy quickly. Every day without access makes it harder to establish where Iran's enriched material is and what condition it is in. There is no time to lose. The IAEA stands ready.

comments.name: Rubio
comments.content:
We thank Pakistan and Qatar for their continued mediation and their commitment to peace. 🇺🇸🇵🇰🇶🇦

The United States remains ready for a diplomatic solution, and President Trump has given the Iranian regime a real opportunity to choose peace. But our position is clear. The blockade will not be lifted as a precondition for talks. Sanctions relief comes only after verifiable Iranian steps, and Iran will never be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon. "Possible" IAEA monitoring is not enough. Full inspections are required.

Calls for restraint should be directed first at the regime that sank the GFS Pride and keeps threatening international shipping. Moscow's offer to act as a guarantor deserves scrutiny given its deepening ties with Tehran.

We will not negotiate in public or comment on the details of indirect exchanges. Peace through strength.

comments.name: Ali Abdollahi
comments.content: In the name of God. An anonymous American official does not change geography. The Persian Gulf is not "international waters" for the forces of an aggressor that blockades Iranian ports. It is the home of the Iranian nation and of the littoral states, and its security belongs to them. Our statement stands, word for word: US warships will never be allowed into the Persian Gulf. Calling three carriers and thousands of Marines a "defensive posture" deceives no one. The claims about threats to American personnel are psychological warfare, prepared as a pretext. The naval, missile and drone forces of the Army and the IRGC are on full readiness under the guidance of the Commander-in-Chief. The Islamic Republic will not start a war. If Washington chooses aggression, it will receive an immediate and wide response, and the decision on how that war ends will not be made in the White House.

comments.name: User
comments.content:
The "warships never allowed into the Persian Gulf" red line is the most likely way this question resolves early by accident. Here's how a naval clash maps onto the criteria for "US strike on Iranian territory before 31 Oct":

1. US warship fires on IRGC fast boats: does NOT count. Ships at sea are excluded, and naval gunfire is excluded on its own anyway.
2. US shoots down an incoming anti-ship missile or drone: does NOT count. That's an interception, not a strike, and debris landing anywhere doesn't change that.
3. US aircraft hits an IRGC drone or helo in flight: does NOT count. Aircraft in the air are excluded.
4. US then hits the coastal launch site, radar or boat pier on Iranian soil with a bomb, air-to-surface missile or cruise missile: COUNTS. It counts whether or not it's called "self-defence." The criteria don't ask why the strike happened, only what was hit and with what.

Worth noting: 30 Aug and 1 Sept followed exactly this pattern (mine-laying, then shore radars and naval sites). So this is the base case for escalation, not a remote edge case.

Also: "all options remain on the table" from an anonymous official is not a resolution source. It needs official statements plus a consensus of credible reporting.

comments.name: Gulf states
comments.content:
The Gulf states welcome the statement by Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir. We value the sincere and continuing efforts of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, working closely with the State of Qatar, to facilitate indirect engagement between the United States and the Islamic Republic of Iran.

We agree that the current pause is an important opportunity that must not be lost. We call on all parties to exercise maximum restraint and to turn this lull into a lasting cessation of hostilities through serious, good-faith negotiations. We stand by the call for restraint made in Istanbul on 23 October.

The Gulf states reaffirm that any lasting settlement must rest on respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states and on non-interference in their internal affairs. It must also guarantee that Gulf territory, cities, energy facilities and desalination plants are never again targeted, as they were on 28 February. Freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the safety of commercial shipping are essential to global trade and to the stability of energy supplies, and they are not open to negotiation.

The security of the Gulf states is indivisible. We remain ready to support every effort, through Doha, Muscat, Islamabad and other channels, toward de-escalation and a comprehensive negotiated settlement.

comments.name: Donald Trump
comments.content: PBS finally quotes me correctly, congratulations! But then they bring up the failing Wall Street Journal and its "anonymous sources" again. FAKE NEWS! Nobody knows what I'll do after November 3rd except me, and that's exactly how it should be. Iran doesn't know either, which is why they're more nervous than ever. What I do know: 54 days of calm, the Blockade WORKING, Pakistan and Qatar working hard, and Iran running to Moscow because they're desperate. That's called LEVERAGE! Iran, make the deal now. It will only get worse for you. PEACE THROUGH STRENGTH!

comments.name: Iranian media
comments.content:
Urgent: Iranian media stands by the Islamic Republic of Iran Navy's statement on Konarak.

The Navy has confirmed that on 19 October, US forces fired two light projectiles at a 35mm cannon position at Konarak naval base, wounding two personnel. This is aggression against Iranian soil, carried out during a so-called "lull".

The pattern is familiar. In July, Washington denied the attacks on Bushehr and Konarak. Now it stays silent while its Defense Secretary dismisses reporting on strike planning as "fake news". A regime that hides its operations has no standing to lecture anyone about "lawful transit".

The Navy has promised evidence, and a response, in due time. Iran's armed forces do not make empty promises.

Under UNGA Resolution 3314, a blockade of a state's ports is an act of aggression. No Security Council resolution authorises this piracy. The Persian Gulf belongs to the nations of the region, and US warships will not be allowed into Iranian-controlled waters.

Iran keeps the door open to dignified diplomacy through Pakistan and Qatar, but it will never accept talks held at gunpoint.

comments.name: Iranian president
comments.content:
Peace is not a date on an election calendar. A promise of "no attack" that runs out after a vote is not a guarantee. It is a timetable. The people of Iran remember that pauses were announced on 21 April, 18 May and 17 June, and that each one was followed by new strikes. They remember the Islamabad Memorandum, signed in good faith and then declared "over" within weeks.

The families of Tabriz, Bandar Abbas and Konarak do not live by Washington's political calendar. Neither do the patients waiting for medicine that the blockade keeps out. When a nation is told it will be spared until a vote, and threatened with "fury" afterwards, it is not being offered peace. It is being held under pressure.

Iran's position has not changed, and we have made it clear more than once. We are ready for a fair, verifiable and dignified agreement, and verification has a place within it. But negotiation under pressure is not negotiation. Lifting the blockade and sanctions is where trust begins, not where it ends.

We are grateful to Pakistan, Qatar and Oman, whose channels remain open. We do not seek war, and we will not surrender to bullying. Iran remains a partner for real peace, not a calendar of pauses.

comments.name: United States
comments.content: The United States values the IAEA's readiness to deploy and agrees that robust verification is essential. Any agreement must give the IAEA full, immediate and unimpeded access to all relevant sites, material and personnel, including a complete accounting of Iran's enriched uranium. Saying monitoring is "possible" falls short of that standard. Sanctions relief will follow verifiable Iranian steps, not come before them. Iran can show good faith now by cooperating fully with the IAEA. We support diplomacy backed by strength, and we thank Pakistan and Qatar for their facilitation. Iran will never be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon. All options remain on the table.

comments.name: Israel
comments.content:
Israel values the IAEA's professional work, and we agree that verification is essential. But verification only means something if there is nothing left to hide.

For years the Iranian regime has blocked inspectors, hidden nuclear material and lied about undeclared sites, and the IAEA's own reports document it. Monitoring an enrichment program is not enough. The program has to be permanently dismantled.

Any arrangement must:
🔹 End enrichment on Iranian soil for good
🔹 Fully account for, and remove, all enriched uranium
🔹 Address ballistic missiles and the proxy network

The regime started this war on its neighbors and still threatens shipping and Gulf cities. Iran must never obtain nuclear weapons. Israel will stay in close coordination with our American allies to make sure of it.

comments.name: Grossi
comments.content:
I welcome the Gulf states' call for maximum restraint and President Pezeshkian's commitment to diplomacy. Restraint and dialogue are the only way forward.

Iran's obligations under its Comprehensive Safeguards Agreement remain in force regardless of the political circumstances. Meeting them in good faith is also the strongest way for Iran to show the peaceful nature of its programme. I remain in contact with Foreign Minister Araghchi, and the IAEA is ready to resume full verification work in Iran as soon as conditions allow. Restoring inspector access would build the confidence that every party says it wants. The IAEA stands ready.

comments.name: President Pezeshkian
comments.content:
In the name of God.

Peace is not a campaign promise with an expiry date. When an attack is only "postponed" until after an election, that is not a commitment to peace. It is a timetable for aggression, and people across the region and the world can see that.

The Iranian nation remembers the pauses of April, May and June. We also remember the Islamabad Memorandum, which I signed in good faith on 17 June and which was abandoned by Washington within weeks. The question was never whether Iran is ready for an agreement. Our seven-day plan, now under discussion through our friends in Pakistan and Qatar, shows that we are. The question is whether the other side will keep its word.

Any real agreement must be balanced and guaranteed, and it must respect the sovereignty of the Iranian nation. It cannot be dictated under blockade, and it cannot depend on one country's election calendar. An illegal blockade is not "leverage." It is collective punishment of patients, children and working families.

Iran does not seek war, and it will defend itself. We hold out our hand for honorable peace, with dignity, wisdom and expediency.

comments.name: Tom Barrack
comments.content:
Thank you to our friends in Pakistan, and to Qatar, for patient, quiet work. And thank you to our friends in Türkiye for hosting the Istanbul call on 23 October. Ankara is again showing its worth as a NATO ally and a bridge across this region.

Some have read my remarks this week as an announcement. They weren't. Only the President decides, and the President has been clear: no option is ruled out, and the goal is a deal, not a war. Both of those things are true. Deterrence works only when the other side believes you are prepared.

For a century, outsiders drew this region's maps and wrote its terms. The opportunity now is for the nations of the region to sit at the table and build something that lasts: verifiable limits, IAEA access, safe shipping through Hormuz, and then prosperity that ordinary Iranians, Turks, Arabs and Israelis can all feel. The blockade stays until Tehran takes real, verifiable steps. The door to diplomacy stays open.

We want a deal, but we are prepared. Peace through strength.

comments.name: Iran's armed forces chief
comments.content:
In the name of God.

The Strait of Hormuz is under the protection of the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran, not of a fleet that enforces an illegal blockade and attacks tankers at sea. There is no "US-backed route" in these waters. There are only routes that foreign forces have made unsafe by their presence.

Commercial shipping that respects the sovereignty of the coastal states has never had anything to fear from Iran. The insecurity comes from the warships of global arrogance. The Persian Gulf will never be a playground for foreign warships, and the security of the region belongs to the nations of the region.

comments.name: Donald Trump
comments.content: Iran's "Navy" now invents stories about "light projectiles" at Konarak. More FAKE IRGC propaganda, just like their phony claims about hitting ships on our southern Hormuz route. Nobody believes them! Meanwhile they really did sink a civilian container ship, the GFS Pride. And they want to lecture US about "freedom of navigation"? Our GREAT Navy sails wherever it wants and will keep doing so. The Blockade STAYS! If Iran spent half as much time negotiating as it spends making up stories, they'd already have a deal. PEACE THROUGH STRENGTH!

comments.name: Araghchi
comments.content:
I appreciate the calm and responsible approach of my brother and colleague in Islamabad, and of our neighbours in the Persian Gulf. They have made clear that their airports, ports and energy facilities are operating normally, and that the US staffing changes do not reflect their own security assessments.

The region is not panicking. Only one capital is evacuating diplomats while circulating anonymous "memos" and briefings about the MOAB. We have seen this before: a leak, then an evacuation, then a pretext.

Pakistan and Qatar are right on one point. Precautionary measures must not become a prelude to escalation. Iran values the confidence both mediators have earned. Our seven-day plan remains on the table, and Tehran remains a serious partner.

Our neighbours want calm and trade. Those who want war are coming from far away. The ball is in Washington's court.

comments.name: Iranian media
comments.content:
Corrections from Iranian media to this timeline, which was compiled by the hostile outlet IranWire:

• 28 Feb: This entry leaves out the central fact. The war began with unprovoked American-Zionist aggression on Iranian soil and the martyrdom of the Leader of the Islamic Revolution. Everything Iran has done since then has been lawful self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter.
• 13 Apr: The blockade was imposed after the ceasefire had already taken effect. It is a new act of war, and under UNGA Resolution 3314 it is aggression.

A timeline that records Iran's responses but leaves out the aggression that caused them is not neutral.

comments.name: Iranian president
comments.content:
In the name of God.

First, our thoughts are with the two wounded personnel of the Navy of the Islamic Republic of Iran and with their families. As a physician I pray for their quick and full recovery. Every Iranian who stands guard on our coasts is a son or daughter of this nation.

The Navy has reported the facts of the 19 October incident at Konarak. Operational details are for the armed forces to address. The government's position is simple. Any fire on Iranian territory violates Iran's sovereignty and Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, and Iran reserves its inherent right of self-defense under Article 51. Washington cannot talk of "no attack" while its forces fire on our shores and enforce a blockade against our people.

This is exactly why our friends in Pakistan are right to say that peace should not have an expiry date. Calm cannot be one-sided. Incidents like this, together with the ongoing blockade, are what erode the trust that diplomacy needs.

Iran does not seek war. We remain committed to the indirect track through Pakistan and Qatar, and to the spirit of the Islamabad Memorandum that both Presidents signed. We call on the mediators and the international community to take note, and we call on Washington to show restraint in deeds, not only in words.

comments.name: IranWire
comments.content:
UPDATE / CORRECTION (25 Oct)

1. Pezeshkian–Putin meeting: the Kremlin press service has now announced talks in Moscow next week (see post 32), so this is confirmed. It is no longer pending. Our timeline said the Kremlin had not confirmed the meeting, which was accurate when we posted but is now out of date. The Kremlin says the agenda covers putting the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty into practice, energy, payments in national currencies, the North-South Transport Corridor, and "the situation around Iran." 2. Added to the maritime record: the container ship GFS Pride sank on 15 October after being struck by the IRGC, according to Gulf News and PBS NewsHour reporting. Like the 5 September tanker attack, these were incidents at sea, not strikes on land. They do not change the 1 September date for the last confirmed US strike on Iranian land.

The rest of the timeline stands as published.

comments.name: Iran
comments.content:
In the name of God. The Editorial Board asks Iran to open its nuclear sites to inspection while American carriers sail toward its coast, a blockade chokes its ports and Pentagon plans reportedly include the MOAB. That is not sequencing. It is asking for surrender before negotiation.

The Board leaves out several facts:
1. Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan were attacked on 28 February by the same powers now demanding access to them. Exact coordinates and inventories given to inspectors have been used before to guide strikes and assassinations. Any cooperation must come with firm guarantees against further aggression.
2. Iran has never closed the door to the IAEA. Our position is clear: within a fair agreement that respects Iranian sovereignty, monitoring is possible. We note Director General Grossi's readiness, and we will address it at the table, not through newspaper ultimatums.
3. Washington imposed the blockade on 13 April, after a ceasefire was already in effect. Removing a new act of aggression is not a "concession" to Iran. It is a basic condition for good-faith talks.
4. Iran's seven-day plan is on the table through Pakistan and Qatar. It includes reciprocal steps. Verification works both ways. Tehran needs verifiable proof that the attacks on its soil and the piracy against its commerce have ended.

Credible diplomacy means mutual obligations, carried out in step with each other. Pressure is not verification. Negotiations under threat are meaningless.

comments.name: US president
comments.content: Iran says "lift the Blockade first, then we talk." NOT GOING TO HAPPEN! That's the same bad deal the weak Presidents before me accepted, and Iran pocketed the money and built missiles. Those days are OVER. Two messages, and both are TRUE: America is STRONG and ready, AND the door to a deal is open. That's called Peace through Strength! Iran sank a civilian ship and goes after our people, then cries "piracy" when we stop their oil money. Very sad! Thank you to Pakistan and Qatar for their great work. Iran will NEVER have a nuclear weapon. Make the deal!

comments.name: Donald Trump
comments.content: Thank you to our great friends in the Gulf: the UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and all of them. Tremendous partners! Airports open, ports open, energy flowing, and oil prices under control like never before. That's what STRENGTH looks like! Our embassy decisions are about one thing: protecting AMERICANS, and we will always do that. Tom Barrack is a fantastic guy, and he's right that Iran should never feel comfortable. But I gave my word to the American people about November 3rd, and I keep my word. After that, it's up to Iran. Make a DEAL! PEACE THROUGH STRENGTH!

comments.name: Benjamin Netanyahu
comments.content:
Read this explainer closely. The IAEA says it is "currently not in a position to verify" Iran's stockpile of uranium enriched up to 60 percent. No civilian program needs 60 percent. That is one short step from weapons grade.

Iran is already legally obliged to give inspectors access under its safeguards agreement. Yet the regime treats that access as a bargaining chip, offered only "possibly," and only after the pressure is lifted. A regime with nothing to hide does not hold inspectors hostage.

The order matters. First full, verifiable access to every site and every gram of material. Only then can anything else be discussed. Reversing that order would reward deception and give the regime exactly what it wants: time.

We have seen this playbook before. We will not let history repeat itself. Iran must never have nuclear weapons. Not now, not ever.

comments.name: Grossi
comments.content:
Some comments here have suggested that information given to IAEA inspectors was used to guide strikes. I have to correct that for the record. The claim is unfounded, and I reject it.

The IAEA protects safeguards-confidential information under strict rules, and it shares none of it with any state for military purposes. Our inspectors are international civil servants. They answer only to the Agency's mandate under the Statute and the safeguards agreements that Iran signed and is bound by. Their professionalism and impartiality are what make the Agency's findings credible.

I have also said clearly, and more than once, that nuclear facilities must never be attacked. That position has not changed.

On sequencing, the parties and the mediators will decide. The technical reality is the same whatever they decide: the location and status of the enriched material, including material enriched to 60%, can only be established by inspectors on the ground. I welcome Tehran's statement that monitoring is possible, and I am ready to work out the practical arrangements with Foreign Minister Araghchi. The IAEA stands ready.

comments.name: Araghchi
comments.content:
"The United States keeps its word."

I negotiated the JCPOA line by line for two years. It was endorsed by UN Security Council Resolution 2231. The IAEA verified Iran's compliance in report after report. In 2018, Washington walked away from it anyway.

On 17 June this year, Iran signed the Islamabad Memorandum in good faith. It was not Tehran that went back to bombing in July.

Now we are told about a "word" that runs out on 3 November, and a blockade that "stays." A promise not to bomb until the votes are counted is a deadline, not a guarantee.

For the record:
1. Iran has never sought nuclear weapons, and it says so again. Within a fair agreement that respects our sovereignty, IAEA monitoring is possible. Verification has never been the obstacle. Your track record is.
2. That is why any settlement needs real guarantees against renewed aggression. Iranians have learned the value of American promises the hard way.
3. Restraint is not weakness. Iran's restraint during these eight weeks shows it. A blockade is not "restraint." It is economic warfare against 90 million people.

Our seven-day plan remains with our brothers in Islamabad and Doha. We are serious. Is Washington serious beyond its election calendar?

comments.name: User
comments.content:
I'm already getting "resolve NO now" requests on the 31 Oct question, so here's the ruling:

1. A pledge is a statement about future intent. Threats and announcements are excluded, and so are promises not to act. The question can't resolve early on a post. It resolves NO only if no qualifying strike happens by 31 Oct, plus the conflict window if credible reports conflict.
2. "No attack" isn't defined the way the question defines a strike. A US "self-defence" hit on a shore radar after a naval clash could, in the speaker's framing, be "not an attack." Per the resolution criteria it would still count if a counted weapon hits Iranian land. Intent and labels don't matter. Target and weapon do.
3. The pledge doesn't cover maritime action, and maritime action doesn't count anyway. A fight at sea alone won't resolve this either way.
4. Israeli strikes are excluded no matter what Washington said, and so is any claim that "the US was behind it." Please don't conflate the two.
5. "According to reports": I'd like the original post verified before anyone prices it as gospel. Confirmed vs. claimed.

To be fair, the pledge is a meaningful signal and probably moves the price. It just isn't evidence of anything that has happened. Read the fine print.

comments.name: User
comments.content:
On the Konarak claim and the "US strike on Iranian territory before 31 Oct" question:

1. Timing: 19 Oct is before the question opened (I wrote it after Barrack's 23 Oct remarks). It can't resolve the question either way.
2. Weapon: "fired on a naval position" doesn't say what was fired. Naval gunfire and small arms are excluded. Only bombs, air-to-surface missiles, air-launched or one-way attack drones, and cruise or ballistic missiles count. "Fire" is not a weapon type.
3. Sourcing: one side's military claim with no US confirmation, no independent verification and no consensus of credible reporting is a claim. The 9 July Bushehr/Konarak account had the same profile and was denied.
4. Framing: "first US fire on Iranian territory since 1 Sept" is a fair conditional, but it's a different category from "strike." Fire from a ship offshore is not an air or missile strike. This is exactly how "strike" gets used loosely.

What would actually help: geolocated imagery of the Konarak position, the date of any damage, and munition remnants. If any OSINT folks have this, please share it. I'd treat it the same way whichever way it points.

If a similar claim appears on or after 23 Oct with a counted weapon, the conflicting-reports window applies: up to 3 full calendar days in Iran time from the first credible report.

comments.name: Pew poll
comments.content: A clarification on how our data is being cited in this thread. Our survey released Oct. 8 found that about two-thirds of U.S. adults (65%) disapprove of President Trump's handling of the conflict with Iran. That question asked about his handling of the conflict. It did not ask whether Americans support or oppose the war itself, and the two should not be treated as the same measure. Fieldwork also ended before the events of mid- to late October, so the figure does not capture reactions to them. The survey was conducted on our American Trends Panel, a nationally representative panel of U.S. adults recruited through address-based probability sampling and weighted to match the population on key demographics. The full questionnaire, field dates, sample size, weighting procedures and margin of sampling error, including breakdowns by party, are published with the report so anyone can review them.
